title: Tail exile: weak cells banished to an SRAM patch
idea: Ideal: a DRAM that never refreshes. Closest: a power-on BIST at elevated wordline-off stress finds the ~0.1% of cells with retention <2 s and stores their addresses in an on-die CAM plus a small SRAM patch that shadows those bits; the other 99.9% of the array is refreshed every 2-4 s instead of every 32-64 ms.
why: Fact 3 (leakage tail forces refresh): refresh energy and refresh bandwidth loss cut ~30-60x for the bulk array at ~0.5% area for the patch; VRT cells handled by periodic re-profiling.

title: Canary cells that decay first and call for refresh
idea: Ideal: memory that knows the instant it starts forgetting. Closest: every subarray carries a few deliberately weakened canary cells (narrower access FET, ~30% smaller Cs, written to '1'); a tiny comparator polls them and the subarray is refreshed only when its canaries droop past a guard threshold, so refresh follows real temperature, voltage and aging per subarray instead of the worst-case corner.
why: Fact 3: removes the 4-8x worst-case guard band in refresh rate; ~50-75% refresh energy cut in typical conditions.

title: Bit-significance tiering: mantissa LSBs live in unrefreshed soft rows
idea: Ideal: errors that cost nothing because they do not matter. Closest: the memory controller splits each bf16/fp8 tensor word, storing sign, exponent and top mantissa bits in refreshed ECC rows and the low mantissa bits in 'soft rows' with 1 s refresh and no ECC, where rare decays add noise below quantization noise.
why: Facts 3 and 1: ~40% of AI tensor bits need no fast refresh or ECC; refresh power ~-35%, ECC overhead removed on that fraction, and soft rows can use smaller Cs.

title: Page-wide LDPC computed in the sense-amp stripe
idea: Ideal: error correction with zero overhead bits. Closest: since every activate already senses an ~8 kb row, add a long-block LDPC code over the whole row (~3% parity versus 12.5% for per-word SECDED) decoded bit-serially in the sense-amp stripe during tRAS, so dozens of marginal cells per row are fixed before any column read.
why: Facts 1, 3, 8: turns the 128x overfetch into an asset; tolerates ~100x higher raw BER at lower parity cost, letting Cs drop ~30% or refresh slow 4-8x.

title: Soft-decision re-sense with shifted bitline references
idea: Ideal: never lose a bit, even when the cell signal is nearly zero. Closest: when the fast decoder fails, the row is re-sensed twice more with the bitline precharge shifted by +/-15 mV, producing per-bit confidence (like NAND read-retry) that feeds a soft-decision decoder able to recover cells with only ~20 mV of signal.
why: Facts 1 and 3: roughly doubles usable cell margin, enabling smaller capacitors or longer refresh at the price of rare slow reads.

title: Moving-target rows: keyed rolling remap defeats hammering
idea: Ideal: hammering is pointless because the aggressor never stays next to its victim. Closest: the DRAM keeps a secret keyed permutation of logical to physical rows and migrates one row per refresh slot to a new physical position, so any logical aggressor's physical neighbors change before ~1k activations can accumulate.
why: Fact 9: makes falling hammer thresholds irrelevant without per-row counters; costs one extra row copy per refresh slot (~1-2% bandwidth).

title: On-die micro-heaters anneal leaky access-transistor traps in the field
idea: Ideal: weak cells repair themselves. Closest: polysilicon heater lines under each mat drive local 250-350 C pulses lasting milliseconds (after migrating that mat's data) to anneal the interface and junction traps behind variable-retention-time and GIDL tail cells, resetting them to their low-leak state.
why: Fact 3: could shrink the leakage tail and VRT population 3-10x so refresh slows proportionally; also extends field life.

title: Per-row trimmed negative wordline for tail rows only
idea: Ideal: zero off-state leakage. Closest: each row gets a 2-bit trim register set at test that picks its standby wordline voltage from -0.2/-0.4/-0.6 V, so rows holding tail cells get deep negative bias (~10x lower subthreshold leakage) while healthy rows stay shallow and avoid the GIDL penalty of deep bias.
why: Fact 3: cuts the leakage of the rows that set refresh by ~10x; refresh interval 2-4x longer at ~1% area.

title: Bit-flip-hardened training so AI memory runs at relaxed refresh
idea: Ideal: the application does not care about memory errors. Closest: train and fine-tune models with injected bit-flip noise matching a 1e-6 raw BER profile, protect only optimizer state and index tensors with CRC, then deploy weights and activations in DRAM running at 8x the normal refresh interval.
why: Fact 3: AI memory (the main demand driver) gets ~80% lower refresh energy and ~10% more bandwidth with <0.1% accuracy loss.

title: Bad-cell-map grade: ship scattered-defect dies with fused bitmaps
idea: Ideal: no die is ever scrapped. Closest: dies failing JEDEC only because of scattered bad cells are sold as a new grade carrying a fused, compressed bad-cell map that the host reads at boot, retiring the affected 4 KB pages or placing error-tolerant tensors there.
why: Supply axis: recovers ~5-15% of wafer output now down-binned or scrapped, raising usable bits with zero new capex.

title: Elastic twin-cell mode switchable per row group
idea: Ideal: every bit is perfectly reliable but density is never wasted. Closest: a mode register lets the OS flip any row group between 1 cell per bit and 2-cell differential per bit (complementary data on the bitline pair), giving ~4x retention and hammer immunity; kernel, page tables and keys go to twin mode while bulk data stays dense.
why: Facts 3 and 9: hardens the ~2-5% of critical data at 2x cost instead of hardening all bits, so the rest of memory can run at relaxed refresh.

title: Compression-funded retention: saved bits buy stronger codes
idea: Ideal: ECC bits are free. Closest: each 64 B line is compressed (base-delta or frequent-pattern); lines that shrink by >=25% store a 4-error-correcting BCH code in the freed space and live in rows refreshed 8x less often, while incompressible lines stay in normal rows with SECDED.
why: Fact 3: on typical data (~60% compressible) refresh energy falls ~50% with no added parity storage.

title: TSV erasure coding replaces HBM spare TSVs and repair
idea: Ideal: TSV defects do not matter. Closest: data across the 1024-bit HBM interface is Reed-Solomon coded in lane groups (e.g., 8 parity lanes per 128), so open or resistive TSVs are corrected on the fly as erasures instead of being repaired with spares and fuses at test.
why: Fact 6: recovers part of the 20-30% stack yield loss and permits finer TSV pitch with higher defect rates for ~6% lane overhead.

title: Hot-row SRAM shock absorber caps physical activations
idea: Ideal: no physical row is ever activated more than a few hundred times per window. Closest: each bank holds a 4-8 row SRAM buffer that captures any row activated more than 64 times in a window; later hits are served from SRAM, so the physical row is never re-opened and cannot hammer its neighbors.
why: Fact 9: removes hammering at the source and cuts hit latency; ~1% die area and no TRR refresh overhead.

title: Sense-settling timer flags marginal bits as erasures
idea: Ideal: knowing exactly which bits are wrong without storing extra bits. Closest: a per-column comparator times how long each sense amp takes to resolve; bits that resolve slowly (small signal) are flagged to the decoder as erasures, and since an erasure costs half an error, a code fixing t errors now fixes 2t marginal bits.
why: Facts 1 and 3: doubles effective ECC strength at no parity cost, allowing ~2x weaker cells or 2-4x longer refresh.

title: Shaped wordline falling edge and capped row-open time
idea: Ideal: activating a row disturbs nothing. Closest: the wordline driver uses a slow, shaped falling ramp (~5 ns) instead of a sharp edge to cut electron injection and capacitive kick into adjacent rows, and the controller closes rows after <=36 ns to avoid RowPress-style long-open disturbance.
why: Fact 9: may raise the effective hammer threshold 3-10x at small latency cost, reducing mitigation refreshes.

title: Fleet error telemetry redeploys aging DIMMs instead of scrapping
idea: Ideal: no DIMM is ever retired early. Closest: hyperscalers pool corrected-error telemetry (per row, bank, temperature) to predict which DIMMs are degrading, then move them to error-tolerant services (caches, AI inference with retries) under stricter scrubbing rather than replacing them, stretching service life from ~5 to ~8 years.
why: Supply axis: effectively adds 20-40% to installed DRAM capacity over a hardware cycle with zero fab capex.

title: Grade-mixed ranks: Reed-Solomon makes one cheap die harmless
idea: Ideal: any die can be used. Closest: a rank uses symbol-level Reed-Solomon over 10 chips with 2 check chips, which lets one chip per rank be a cheap C-grade die with raw BER ~1e-5 (treated as a known-unreliable symbol) while the module still meets server RAS targets.
why: Supply and cost: absorbs down-binned dies into server modules, lowering module cost ~10-15%.

title: Recompute-as-correction for KV caches and activations
idea: Ideal: memory errors are free to fix because the data can be regenerated. Closest: AI KV-cache and activation buffers are stored in unprotected relaxed-refresh DRAM with only a 16-bit CRC per 1 KB block; on a CRC miss the runtime recomputes that block from upstream tokens or layers instead of correcting it.
why: Facts 3 and 5: removes ECC storage and most refresh for the largest AI memory consumer; recompute costs <0.1% of FLOPs at 1e-7 block error rates.

title: Resonant-tunneling-diode latch makes the DRAM cell bistable
idea: Ideal: a capacitor cell that never needs refresh. Closest: a pair of series resonant tunneling diodes on each storage node forms a negative-differential-resistance bistable that holds the node at '0' or '1' against leakage with picoamp standby current, while the cell is still read and written through its single access transistor.
why: Fact 3: eliminates refresh entirely (46 fJ/bit, 16-33% of idle power) if RTD peak-to-valley ratios can be made uniform across billions of cells.

title: ML-grade memory class with declared raw BER
idea: Ideal: fabs build cells exactly as weak as the workload can tolerate. Closest: JEDEC/OCP define an ML-grade memory class that declares raw BER and retention distribution and mandates host-side strong ECC, so fabs can relax the capacitor target from ~5 fF to ~3 fF and ship parts that today fail retention screens.
why: Fact 1: relaxing Cs ~40% lowers pillar aspect ratio from ~70:1 toward ~45:1, cutting etch difficulty and yield loss while adding supply.

title: Tier-RAID for 3D DRAM tolerates weak lateral transistors
idea: Ideal: 3D DRAM where bad tiers do not matter. Closest: stack 36 tiers of which 4 are parity tiers, stripe each logical row across tiers under an erasure code, and let tiers whose lateral transistors show 100x worse leakage tails be declared erased between refreshes rather than refreshed faster.
why: Fact 2: relaxes the lateral-transistor specs that block 3D manufacturability and may pull 3D break-even earlier at ~11% overhead.

title: Lifetime-tagged allocation skips refresh for short-lived data
idea: Ideal: no refresh because data dies before it decays. Closest: allocators tag buffers with expected lifetime (activations, packets, frame buffers); rows holding only data due to be overwritten within the retention guarantee are excluded from refresh by a per-row skip bit set by the controller.
why: Fact 3: in AI and streaming workloads ~50% of rows hold data living <64 ms, so refresh energy and bandwidth fall ~50%.

title: 180 nm RAS hub chip lets leading-edge dies ship raw
idea: Ideal: the DRAM die is pure array and all reliability logic is free. Closest: a buffer chip built in a fully depreciated 180 nm US fab sits on each DIMM and performs page-level BCH, a bad-row remap CAM and hammer tracking for 8-16 dies, so memory makers can drop on-die ECC and ship dies through relaxed retention screens.
why: Facts 7 and 3 plus U.S. manufacturability: moves ~5-10% of die area off leading-edge silicon onto 180 nm tools and raises sellable yield.

title: Leaky-capacitor integrators count hammer activations automatically
idea: Ideal: hammer counting that needs no counter memory. Closest: a 180 nm companion chip holds an array of MOS capacitors, one per row group, each receiving a fixed charge packet per ACT and leaking with a time constant equal to the refresh window, so each voltage is a free sliding-window activation count; a comparator fires neighbor refresh at threshold.
why: Fact 9: analog decay implements the sliding window that digital trackers spend kilobytes of SRAM on; ~10x less area than counter tables.

title: Four-level cells in fat 180 nm capacitors rescued by soft ECC
idea: Ideal: twice the bits from the same old cell. Closest: 180 nm stacked capacitors hold ~25-30 fF, enough charge for 4 levels at ~250 mV spacing; store 2 bits per cell with a three-reference sense amp and absorb the higher raw error rate with a page-level soft-decision BCH code.
why: Density and U.S. manufacturability: doubles bits per mm2 on legacy US lines with zero EUV.

title: High-pressure deuterium anneal passivates leakage-tail traps
idea: Ideal: an access transistor with zero interface traps. Closest: finish wafers with a high-pressure (5-20 atm) deuterium furnace anneal, a mid-1990s finding, because Si-D bonds resist thermal and hot-carrier breakage far better than Si-H, so trap-assisted junction leakage and VRT cells are passivated more completely and stay passivated.
why: Fact 3: possibly 2-5x fewer tail cells and longer refresh intervals using existing furnaces.

title: Wafer-scale 180 nm DRAM with mesh self-routing around defects
idea: Ideal: 100% yield without a perfect fab. Closest: build an entire 200 mm wafer as one memory module of ~2,000 subarray tiles linked by a redundant mesh; a boot-time BIST disables bad tiles and soft-routes around them, so random defects only remove capacity and never kill the part.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: turns old 180 nm lines into high-capacity modules with no die sort, dicing or per-die packaging.

title: SIMOX-isolated access transistors remove junction leakage tail
idea: Ideal: a storage node with no leakage path to the substrate. Closest: build the cell array on 1990s SIMOX silicon-on-insulator so the storage-node junction sits on buried oxide, eliminating the substrate junction area and deep-level-defect generation current that create most retention tail cells.
why: Fact 3: junction-leakage tail cut perhaps ~10x, tightening retention spread so refresh runs 4-10x less often.

title: MeV-implant proximity gettering under the array
idea: Ideal: silicon with no metal impurities near the storage node. Closest: a high-energy (MeV) carbon or silicon implant places a damage layer ~2-3 um below the array that traps iron, nickel and copper during later anneals, removing the deep-level generation centers behind tail cells.
why: Fact 3: shrinks the defect-driven tail, possibly 2-4x longer worst-case retention, using 1990s MeV implanters.

title: Liquid-nitrogen DRAM vault where cells never forget
idea: Ideal: memory that never forgets. Closest: run 180 nm-era DRAM dies immersed at 77 K, where subthreshold and junction leakage fall by many orders so retention reaches hours, refresh disappears and the tail vanishes; the vault serves as a large refresh-free capacity tier.
why: Fact 3 and supply: refresh-free and tail-free on legacy fabs; cryocooling cost is partly offset by the removed refresh and relaxed cell design.

title: Crossbar parity mats: a 2D product code built into geometry
idea: Ideal: error correction as part of the array geometry, with no decoder. Closest: each 180 nm mat reserves one parity row and one parity column maintained by XOR trees in the sense-amp and column stripes, so any single bad cell sits at the intersection of a failing row parity and a failing column parity and is flipped back.
why: Facts 1 and 3: corrects isolated weak cells at ~3% overhead with trivial logic, allowing relaxed cell specs.

title: Leakage-clocked refresh: a diode array runs the refresh oscillator
idea: Ideal: refresh exactly as often as the physics demands, never more. Closest: a large reverse-biased diode array of the same junction type as the storage nodes discharges a timing capacitor that clocks the refresh counter, so the refresh rate follows temperature, process and aging automatically with plain 1990s analog parts.
why: Fact 3: removes the worst-case temperature guard band; ~2-4x fewer refreshes on average.

title: Bitline charge recycling between paired subarrays during refresh
idea: Ideal: refresh costs zero energy. Closest: at the end of each refresh, the high bitlines of one subarray dump half their charge through a 180 nm transfer switch into the bitlines of the next subarray to be refreshed, so each refresh reuses roughly half of the previous one's CV2.
why: Facts 3 and 10: refresh energy ~-40% without lowering the voltage floor.

title: Decay-direction coding: store mostly safe bits, detect with Berger
idea: Ideal: data that cannot decay. Closest: each word is stored inverted (with a flag bit) whenever that leaves fewer cells in the leaky charged state; rows that end up fully discharged skip refresh, and because the remaining errors are unidirectional (charged to discharged only) a cheap Berger count code detects every one of them.
why: Fact 3: halves worst-case leaky bits, skips refresh on sparse rows and swaps SECDED for ~log2(n) check bits.

title: Conveyor memory: data circulates so refresh and scrub are inherent
idea: Ideal: memory that is always being read, so always fresh and always checked. Closest: a 180 nm shift-loop DRAM in which every row's data circulates through a sense-and-ECC station every few milliseconds, so refresh and scrubbing happen as a side effect of motion, with many short loops keeping average access near 100 ns.
why: Fact 3: no separate refresh scheduling and errors are corrected before they accumulate; suits a bulk refresh-tolerant tier.

title: Per-mat triple-well back-bias tuned to each mat's leakage mix
idea: Ideal: every mat sits at its own minimum-leakage point. Closest: put each mat in its own 1990s triple-well island with a small local charge pump, and set its substrate bias at test to balance subthreshold leakage (wants deeper bias) against junction and GIDL leakage (wants shallower bias) for that mat's measured tail.
why: Fact 3: per-mat optimization narrows the retention tail ~2-3x versus one chip-wide VBB.

title: Decay-as-scaling: analog weight memory that neural nets self-correct
idea: Ideal: decay that does not change the answer. Closest: store neural-net weights as analog charge in large 180 nm capacitors; cells in a row decay by nearly the same exponential factor, a uniform scaling that a per-row reference cell measures and normalization layers cancel, so only cell-to-cell mismatch counts as error.
why: Facts 3 and 5: removes refresh for slowly changing weights and stores ~4-6 effective bits per cell on legacy tools.

title: Triple-row activation turns charge sharing into majority vote
idea: Ideal: redundancy computed for free by physics. Closest: in a 180 nm array each critical bit is written to three rows on the same bitlines; a read opens all three wordlines at once so charge sharing settles the bitline to the analog majority, masking any one decayed or flipped cell with no logic.
why: Fact 3: a 2-of-3 tolerant tier whose refresh can run ~10x slower; 3x area but zero ECC logic.

title: Error concealment: interpolate uncorrectable words from neighbors
idea: Ideal: errors that are invisible. Closest: a 180 nm memory-side controller tags image, audio and tensor regions; when a word there is uncorrectable it substitutes the average of neighboring elements, as video decoders conceal lost macroblocks, instead of raising a machine check.
why: Fact 3: tolerates ~1e-6 raw BER on media and AI tensors, enabling relaxed refresh and weaker cells for those regions.

title: Hot-air rework refurbishes failed DIMMs at chip granularity
idea: Ideal: no DRAM chip is ever wasted. Closest: decommissioned and failed server DIMMs pass through 1990s-era BGA rework stations and memory testers; the single faulty package is swapped for a harvested good one and the module is re-certified with a lower-speed or extra-scrub profile.
why: Supply: returns ~70-80% of failed DIMMs to service (most failures are one chip), adding capacity at a fraction of new cost.

title: BiCMOS bipolar sense amps read half-charge cells
idea: Ideal: a sense amp that sees any charge. Closest: use 1990s BiCMOS processes to build the sense amps from bipolar differential pairs, whose Vbe matching (~1 mV offset versus 10-20 mV for MOS) lets cells that have lost half their charge still read correctly.
why: Facts 1 and 3: ~2x signal margin lets refresh slow ~2x or Cs drop by about half.

title: Defect-aware coset coding makes weak cells store their safe value
idea: Ideal: defects that happen to store the right value. Closest: the encoder knows each row's weak-cell positions from a BIST map and, using Kuznetsov-Tsybakov coding for memories with defects, picks one of several coset encodings so every weak cell holds the value it decays toward; a few index bits per block replace remapping.
why: Fact 3: neutralizes known tail cells with ~2-4% overhead and no spare rows, using simple 180 nm logic.

title: Pointer residues: self-healing data structures on unprotected memory
idea: Ideal: data structures that heal themselves. Closest: runtimes put a 16-bit residue code of each 48-bit pointer in its unused upper bits and keep redundant back-links, so a corrupted pointer is detected on dereference and rebuilt from its partner; it runs on 1990s-class CPUs with no new silicon.
why: Fact 3: protects the control state that makes bit flips fatal, so bulk memory can run without ECC or at relaxed refresh.

title: Gated-diode self-restoring cell refreshed by one global pulse
idea: Ideal: every cell refreshes itself at once with no sensing. Closest: add a small transistor whose gate is the storage node, in series with a poly diode from a global pulse line; when the line pulses high, cells holding '1' turn the transistor on and top themselves up while '0' cells stay off, so the whole array refreshes in one pulse.
why: Fact 3: replaces row-by-row refresh (bandwidth loss, ~46 fJ/bit) with a global pulse of a few fJ/bit; buildable at 180 nm.

title: Hammer-proof legacy tier for page tables and keys
idea: Ideal: hammering cannot hurt what matters. Closest: page tables, kernel structures and crypto keys live in a small 180 nm DRAM or SRAM tier whose wide cell spacing makes it physically immune to row hammer, so the dense main memory can drop costly TRR to cheap probabilistic neighbor refresh backed by ordinary ECC.
why: Fact 9: removes the privilege-escalation risk that forces aggressive mitigation; recovers ~5-10% of main-memory bandwidth and refresh energy.
